Mount Aconcagua is the highest peak in South America at twenty-two thousand eight hundred thirty-eight feet, standing in the Andes on the Argentina-Chile border. Its name comes from Quechua words meaning stone sentinel. Though lower than the Himalayan giants, the combination of extreme altitude, thin air, cold, and remote location makes it a significant mountaineering objective. The standard route, called Ruta Normal, is non-technical but exposed, and acclimatization is the primary challenge at such extreme altitude. Matthias Zurbriggen led the first European ascent in eighteen ninety-seven. The climbing season is brief, running only from December through February in the Southern Hemisphere summer, and severe weather, cold, and wind make climbing dangerous despite the straightforward routes. Aconcagua has become a frequent third summit for climbers pursuing the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent. The mountain's accessibility to South American populations and its place in this climbing canon have cemented its prominence.
